newsitem.title: UK: IEA says absence of Q1 stockdraw is bearish for oil.
newsitem.headline: IEA says absence of Q1 stockdraw is bearish for oil.

text.p: Oil prices may fall later this year because mild winter weather has left oil inventories untouched at a time when they are normally drawn, said the International Energy Agency (IEA) on Thursday.
The absence of a stockdraw in the first quarter this year is seen as a "bearish signal" for oil markets for the remainder of the year, the IEA said in it's latest Monthly Oil Market Report.
Oil inventories were not drawn even though there was a much smaller than expected rise in oil supply during the same period, it added.
Industry stocks in OECD countries fell by 70,000 barrels per day (bpd) but government stocks and stocks held on oil tankers rose by 10,000 bpd and 125,00 bpd respectively.
Such a small stockdraw has not been seen since 1990.
The stocks held on ships reflected growing volumes of long-haul oil moving between regions in recent months.

The pattern over the past few years has been for inventories to be drawn at between one million bpd and 1.5 million bpd in the first quarter due to demand for winter heating in the northern hemisphere.
There are two reasons for last winter's comparatively low stockdraw -- a looser supply/demand balance and the low inventory level which might have inhibited a further stock draw, said the IEA.
For the first time since mid-1995 total industry stocks on a days forward demand basis are now higher than a year earlier in all three major regions.
Industry stocks in the OECD actually rose by 500,000 bpd in March as rising crude oil and "other oil" stocks more than offset falls in gasoline, distillate and fuel oil.
The build was highest in North America with minimal stock changes in other areas - Europe and the Pacific.
Mild weather and weak demand in all three regions resulted in very small product stock declines compared to a typical March stockdraw.
Although gasoline stocks were unchanged in Europe and the Pacific, the fell 200,000 bpd in North America.
Distillate stocks continued the seasonal decline in North America and the Pacific but European distillate stocks were unchanged.
The actual level of stocks, rather than the rate at which they change, has been running above year ago levels since January -- and the difference has been growing.
At the end of March industry stocks stood at 2384 million barrels, some 99 million barrels above year ago levels.
Levels were higher in all three regions but the biggest difference was in Europe where stocks were 7.4 percent higher.
In North America and the Pacific they were 2.5 percent and 2.1 percent higher respectively.
Middle distillates and residual fuel oil stocks were largely responsible for the difference in all three regions.
Turning to changes within each of the three regions, the IEA said that North American stocks rose by 300,000 bpd in March.
The large rise in refinery throughputs and the fall in oil production were more than offset by higher crude oil imports, causing crude oil stocks to rise by 300,000 bpd.
Crude oil stocks ended the month some five million barrels above March 1996 levels but were still some 30 million below the average for the 1991 to 1995 end of March levels.
Gasoline stocks remained well below the previous five years' levels but the stockdraw in March was only about half the normal rate.
As with gasoline, the stockdraw for middle distillates was much smaller than in earlier years.
In Europe total oil stocks went up by 100,000 bpd during March. This was entirely due to the rise in crude oil stocks which ended the month 11 million barrels higher than a year earlier.

Pacific crude oil stocks rose 100,000 bpd while oil products were virtually unchanged. As in the other two regions middle distillates showed a much smaller fall than usual due to mild weather and weak demand.
